121.quote_or_event: “My own Self is the river Vaitaraṇî, my own Self the Śâlmalî tree; my own Self is the miraculous cow Kâmaduh, my own Self the park Nandana. My own Self is the doer and undoer of misery and happiness; my own Self, friend and foe, according as I act well or badly.”
121.explanation: The monk Anāthi tells King Śreṇika that the soul itself becomes the hell-river and thorn-tree of the damned or the wish-cow and paradise-garden of the gods, depending on how it governs its own conduct.
121.tie_back: Like the Kural, it makes self-command the only thing that decides whether a person rises to the realm of the gods or sinks into the darkness of hell.
121._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; the heaven-or-hell polarity matches closely, though in Jainism gods' heavens are themselves still within saṃsāra, below liberation.

122.quote_or_event: “Subdue your Self, for the Self is difficult to subdue; if your Self is subdued, you will be happy in this world and in the next.”
122.explanation: The first lecture of the Uttarādhyayana presents self-subjugation as the hardest task and the surest source of well-being in both lives.
122.tie_back: Valluvar tells us to guard restraint as our treasure since no greater good exists for a living being; Mahāvīra's verse likewise makes the subdued self the source of happiness here and hereafter.
122._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; matches the value claim strongly but lacks the Kural's image of restraint as wealth to be guarded.

123.quote_or_event: “An intelligent man who has learned (the sacred texts) takes his duties upon himself, and he becomes renowned in the world; as the earth is the dwelling of all beings, so he will be a dwelling of all duties.”
123.explanation: In the lecture on discipline, the pupil who joins learning to disciplined, willing conduct gains renown and becomes a support for every duty.
123.tie_back: The Kural promises distinction, recognized by the good, to one who knows what true knowledge is and is restrained in the right way; this verse likewise pairs learning with disciplined conduct and promises renown.
123._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; a solid thematic fit (knowledge plus discipline bringing renown), but the verse speaks of a monk's duties rather than restraint in general.

124.quote_or_event: “By possession of conduct he obtains a stability like that of the king of mountains (viz. Mêru), whereby a houseless monk destroys the four remnants of Karman which even a Kêvalin possesses.”
124.explanation: Mahāvīra's catalogue of spiritual exertions teaches that steady conduct gives the soul the immovability of Mount Meru, the axis of the Jain cosmos, and carries it to liberation.
124.tie_back: Valluvar says the stature of one who stays restrained without swerving is greater than a mountain; the Jain text uses the greatest mountain of all, Meru, as the image for the person firm in conduct.
124._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; the mountain image and the idea of unswerving conduct match closely, though Jacobi's text speaks of stability rather than height.

125.quote_or_event: King Śreṇika, ruler of Magadha and owner of horses, elephants, a city and a harem, first mocks a young monk and offers him pleasures, then is so taught by him that he begs forgiveness: “When the lion of kings had thus, with the greatest devotion, praised the lion of houseless monks, he, together with his wives, servants, and relations, became a staunch believer in the Law, with a pure mind.”
125.explanation: The richest king of the age bows his head before a monk with no possessions, and the canon presents this humility as his true gain.
125.tie_back: The Kural says humility suits everyone but shines as a second wealth in the wealthy; Śreṇika's bow before the penniless sage is a canonical picture of exactly that.
125.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 20.2, 20.14–15 and 20.54–59, quoting 20.58 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895)
125._accuracy_note: Verse 20.58 verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; a narrative illustration of a powerful man's humility rather than a stated maxim about the wealthy.

126.quote_or_event: “As a tortoise withdraws his limbs within his own body, even so does the valiant withdraw his mind within himself from all sins. He also withdraws his hands, legs, mind, sense-organs, sinful moods, evil words, pride, and deceitfulness. This indeed is the valor of the valiant.”
126.explanation: The Sūtrakṛtāṅga uses the tortoise drawing in its limbs as the model for the heroic ascetic who withdraws the senses, speech and passions from sin.
126.tie_back: This is the Kural's own image: drawing in the five senses like a tortoise its limbs, which in Jain terms stops the inflow (āsrava) of karma that would bind the soul over many births.
126.source: Sūtrakṛtāṅga 1.8.16–18, English rendering as given on Jainworld, 'Jina Sutra – Quotations'
126._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on jainworld.com (not Jacobi's wording); the tortoise simile is a near one-to-one match, though Gita 2.58 and the Kumma Sutta share it, so it is a shared Indian image.

127.quote_or_event: “By watchfulness of speech he keeps free from prevarication; thereby he enables his mind to act properly.”
127.explanation: Vāg-gupti, the guarding of speech, is one of the three Jain guptis (guards of mind, speech and body); the Uttarādhyayana says that guarding the tongue keeps one from falsehood and steadies the mind.
127.tie_back: Valluvar ranks the tongue above every other thing a person must guard; Jain discipline likewise makes guarding speech one of the three basic protections of the soul.
127._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; the doctrine of vāg-gupti fits well, but the verse does not rank the tongue above other guards or speak of the grief of the unguarded.

128.quote_or_event: “One may have a tuft or matted hair on the head or a shaven head, remain naked or wear a rag. But if he tells a lie, all this is futile or fruitless.”
128.explanation: The Digambara text Bhagavatī Ārādhanā teaches that a single untruth empties every outward austerity of its worth.
128.tie_back: Valluvar says one harmful word turns all a person's good to no good; this verse makes the same asymmetric claim, that one false word cancels all accumulated religious effort.
128.source: Bhagavatī Ārādhanā 843 (Śivārya), English rendering as given on Jainworld, 'Jina Sutra – Quotations'
128._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on jainworld.com; strong match on the 'one word cancels all good' logic, though it concerns lying specifically rather than every harmful word.

129.quote_or_event: “One can bear all kinds of unbearable pain caused by spikes in expectation of wealth etc. But he alone who tolerates, without any motive of worldly gain, harsh words spoken to him is venerable.”
129.explanation: The Daśavaikālika sets harsh words beside iron spikes and treats bearing harsh words as the harder test; the next verse in the same lesson (9.3.7) goes on to contrast iron thorns, which are pulled out, with thorns of speech that stay and breed enmity.
129.tie_back: Like Valluvar's fire-burn that heals and tongue-burn that never does, the Jain text ranks the wound of harsh words above physical injury.
129.source: Daśavaikālika Sūtra 9.3.6, English rendering as given on Jainworld, 'Jina Sutra – Quotations'
129._accuracy_note: 9.3.6 verified verbatim on jainworld.com; the paraphrase of 9.3.7 (verbal thorns hard to extract) could not be checked against a live English translation in this session and should be confirmed.

130.quote_or_event: “By conquering anger he obtains patience; he acquires no Karman productive of anger, and destroys the Karman he had acquired before.”
130.explanation: In the same lecture, acquiring sacred knowledge 'destroys ignorance' (29.24), and conquering anger, pride, deceit and greed (29.67–70) leads the soul step by step toward liberation.
130.tie_back: The Kural's three conditions, guarding against anger, learning and being restrained, map onto these Jain steps, and the good that 'waits' for such a person corresponds to the karmic release they bring.
130._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; anger-conquest plus learning fits well, but the Kural's personified Virtue seeking out the restrained person has no Jain counterpart.
